source_span: continuation of the normalisation after the financial repression of the 2010s... I would expect our rates strategists to continue leaning towards higher yields absent a major shock, such as a recession or an AI-led equity bust
source_chain: Global yields are rising due to structural normalization/term-premium after the 2010s repression, not yet a fiscal-panic sell-off, THEREFORE DB's own rates desk still expects yields to keep climbing from here, THEREFORE because current levels now carry much more coupon cushion than in the low-rate 2020s (10Y could reach ~5.5% in a year / ~6.4% in two before total returns turn negative), holding duration is no longer as painful as before, even as yields rise further. Invalidation: a recession or an AI-led equity bust (the only scenario where DB does not expect continued higher yields).
pulse_chain: Warsh's Jackson Hole pivot flips the market from pricing cuts to pricing a hike, driving a global bond selloff, THEREFORE Deutsche Bank's 'bull case' says this is just normalization back toward a pre-2010 norm, not a crisis, and 10-year holders bought at the late-2023 low are still up ~16% — implying the sell-off is benign, THEREFORE an unnamed 'counter' camp (deficits/energy/AI capital) says the direction is structurally higher and wins the next few weeks because a hike is imminent. Invalidation: the September FOMC fails to deliver the priced hike, or Warsh softens his tone.
why: DB's note is not a bond-bullish counterweight to the 'structurally higher' camp — it explicitly says DB's own rates strategists still expect yields to keep rising and names a recession/AI-bust as the only thing that changes that, so the pulse recasts DB's carry-cushion argument as an opposing 'bull case' and swaps in a hike-related invalidation DB never states.
